evidence_set: In a 15-day residential study of 7 volunteers given oral methamphetamine 5 mg twice a day for three days and 10 mg twice a day for three days (blocks on days 4-6 and 10-12; four took the lower dose first, three the higher), ratings of 'good drug effect' (F(1,48)=8.0) and 'high' (F(1,48)=15.0) were raised above the matched placebo baseline day only on the first day of the larger dose and had returned to baseline by day 3; the smaller dose did not differ from baseline on either rating. The two printed P values are transposed relative to their F values (editors' calculation).

Over the same three days the unwanted effects went the other way: dizziness (F=9.8) and flu-like symptoms (F=13.2) rose on day 3 but not day 1, and being unable to concentrate, chills, confusion, depression, nausea and 'bad drug effect' (F=17.4) became significant only on day 3, while 'heart pounding' and 'trouble sleeping' were raised on all three days. Sleep was disrupted mainly on the first night (total sleep time F=12.5, non-REM F=8.2, sleep efficiency F=8.1 and movements F=15.4 on that night only; self-estimated hours slept also fell on night 2, F=7.4), which the authors also read as tolerance; there was no rebound on the placebo days after.

The fall in food intake was sustained across the three days: total daily intake was lower than the placebo baseline by approximately 1150 kcal at 5 mg twice daily and 1450 kcal at 10 mg twice daily (the authors' round figures; the day-by-day gaps in Figure 3 vary around them), significantly on each of days 1, 2 and 3 (F(1,48)=19.2, 44.4 and 29.9; 62.7, 43.9 and 39.6; all P<0.0001), and intake was still below baseline on the first placebo day after each block.
Results > Food intake, 1st paragraph (p. 401, left column); Figure 3 (p. 401)

In the pharmacokinetic arm of the same 13-day regimen (8 men in all: 6 at each challenge dose of 0.125 and 0.250 mg/kg, four of them in both studies about 3 months apart), absorption, apparent clearance, renal clearance, the elimination rate constant and the half-life were unchanged between day 1 and day 15; the only significant changes were upward (peak concentration about 12.5% higher at the larger challenge dose). The printed power analysis gives detectable differences of 21.2% and 14.8% for the elimination rate constant, 18.3% and 6.1% for peak concentration and 20.1% and 15.6% for exposure (lower and higher challenge dose), which the authors describe as a 20% difference being detectable, so the fading response is not explained by faster clearance.
Results > Pharmacokinetic Analysis, last paragraph (p. 859, continuing p. 860); Discussion, 3rd paragraph (p. 860, into the right column); Table 2 (p. 861)

In 9 men given oral methamphetamine 10 mg three times over about 36 hours in a residential laboratory, alone or with alcohol, the heart-rate area under the curve was significantly smaller at the third administration than at the first for both methamphetamine-alcohol conditions (F(3,24)=15.4-26.5, p<0.0001, d=0.8-1.6), and only the larger-alcohol combination still exceeded either drug alone. Blood-pressure effects were unchanged across administrations. The first administration was in the morning of day 2 and the third in the evening of day 3, after one night of drug-disturbed sleep, which the authors name as alternatives to tolerance.
Results > Tolerance > Cardiovascular and BAL effects; Figure 4 (left panel); Discussion, 3rd paragraph; Methods and materials > Design, Table 2 (timing of administrations)

evidence_set: Table 2, MDMA and MDA rows (p. 370); Results > Pharmacokinetics, 2nd paragraph (p. 369, right column)

Results > Pharmacological effects, the paragraphs on physiological parameters (p. 367, right column) and on Maddox wing and hormones (p. 369); Discussion, the paragraph beginning 'The pharmacological effects after the second administration' (starts p. 372, quoted text on p. 373)

Taking 50 mg two hours before a 100 mg dose raised peak MDMA concentration to 311.16 ng/mL (SD 66.48) from 202.92 (SD 30.30) with 100 mg alone (p<0.001), 12.8% above dose proportionality in peak and 16.2% in exposure, with half-life unchanged (10.48 h against 10.41). Heart rate did not differ in peak or area under the curve with the added dose (peak 33.05, SD 13.25, against 33.50, SD 11.87; area under the curve 69.98 against 57.75, neither significant), although it differed at 2.3 and 5 hours of the time course (p=0.004), and none of the wanted subjective effects differed in peak or area under the curve.

A 60 mg booster two hours after 120 mg lengthened the duration of 'any drug effect' to 5.6 h (SD 1.8) from 4.6 h with the single dose (SD 1.2 and p = 0.001 in the abstract and text; SD 1.5 and p<0.01 in Table 1) and raised the areas under several effect curves, while peak ratings did not differ (83, SD 21, against 85, SD 20 for 'any drug effect'; 86, SD 29, against 87, SD 19 for 'good drug effect'). Peak plasma concentration rose 1.50-fold (90% CI 1.43-1.57) and 9-hour exposure 1.47-fold (1.40-1.54), with half-life 7.2 h in both conditions.

Blood pressure, heart rate, rate-pressure product and body temperature rose under both MDMA conditions against placebo and lasted longer after the booster without a higher maximum; the authors say the unchanged maxima despite higher concentrations are consistent with acute pharmacodynamic tolerance, noting that effects subsided within the 9-hour session while the mean concentration at discharge after the booster exceeded the mean peak after the single dose. The numerical autonomic values are in a supplement that the first reader did not open.

evidence_set: The review states that no laboratory study has given a series of MDMA doses to humans and that chronic tolerance therefore cannot be investigated in humans under double-blind, placebo-controlled conditions, so all human evidence comes from surveys of people who use ecstasy recreationally; in those surveys 58% (n=596) of 1151 people surveyed reported tolerance (596 is 52% of 1151, so what the 58% is a percentage of is unclear) and about 85-95% of 430 people using it regularly reported declining subjective efficacy, with an earlier survey finding 67% of those with six or more occasions reporting that positive effects decreased and negative effects increased.

evidence_set: All ten men met the criteria for hypertension (above 140/90 mm Hg) in the study, a statement the paper does not tie to one condition; with 50 mg two hours before 100 mg, the systolic area under the curve over the 2-6 hour window was 72.96 (SD 22.12) against 49.35 (SD 24.28) for 100 mg alone (p=0.029) and the diastolic 46.82 (SD 27.82) against 18.81 (SD 21.09) (p=0.015), while heart rate did not differ in peak or area under the curve.
Table 1, SBP and DBP rows (p. 887); Results > Physiological measures, 1st paragraph (p. 887, bottom left into top right)

With a 60 mg booster two hours after 120 mg, blood pressure, heart rate, rate-pressure product and temperature lasted longer than with the single dose but did not reach higher maxima, and no participant exceeded 180 mm Hg systolic or 40 degrees Celsius. Acute complaint scores did not differ significantly between booster and single dose (22, SD 15, against 20, SD 13), although two of 25 participants, both women receiving the booster as their first MDMA experience, left the study after headache and nausea followed by weeks to months of mental instability (anxiety in both; confusion and impaired concentration in one, restlessness and tension in the other), and are excluded from that comparison.

evidence_set: In a broader sample of 3,810,747 people enrolled for at least 2 years, adjusted relative risks were 1.66 (1.64–1.69) for intermittent and 1.61 (1.58–1.63) for chronic opioid prescriptions. A residual-confounding analysis assumed a binary confounder in 75% of concurrent users and 0% of people without concurrent use. The authors state that unobserved confounding cannot be excluded, that only hospital-treated events in people who survived were counted, and that heroin and illegally bought prescription drugs are not captured.

evidence_set: Of 399,230 US opioid-involved poisoning deaths in 1999–2017, the share whose death certificates also named benzodiazepines rose from 8.7% in 1999 to 26.2% in 2010 and fell to 21.0% in 2017; death rates for opioid overdoses involving benzodiazepines rose 10.3-fold, against 5.0-fold for all opioid overdose deaths. By subtype: heroin 4.0% (1999) to 17.1% (2017; the abstract gives 17.1% for synthetic opioids in 2017 instead); methadone 15.6% (2000) to 32.0% (2017); prescription opioids 15.6% (2000) to 33.1% (2017); synthetic opioids between 15.0% and 25.9%.
